title: Offline Channel-Independent QAOA Angles for RIS Power Aggregation: Unit-Circle Phase Dictionaries and Infinite-Size Spin-Glass Limits
abstract: Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) maximize received power by setting per-element phases. Discrete-phase optimization is NP-hard in the worst case, while the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) applied to RIS faces limited phase alphabets, either per-problem angle optimization or uncharacterized training cost exposed to barren plateaus, and no scalable performance benchmark. We introduce a $2^{M}$-phase $θ$ dictionary for optimizing power $\|\mathbf{A} \, e^{jθ}\|^{2}$ having $K \times N$ channel matrix $\mathbf{A}$ and QAOA angle offline optimization with instance and size-independent infinite-size limit of the mixed-$q$ Gaussian ensemble of Basso et al. Our design bounds the spin-Hamiltonian interaction order to at most quartic for any $M$, and the deployed order-2 reduction lies below the even-$q\!\ge\!4$ regime in which constant-level QAOA limitations are proved. We perform analytical, state-vector, matrix-product-state and Pauli-path-simulation numerical studies for $N=K \leq 100$ and QAOA depth $p=9$, verifying offline angle transfer to Rayleigh, Rician/line-of-sight, cascaded double-fading and spatially-correlated RIS channels at $N\!\in\!\{5,12\}$. We observe performance reaching a near-optimal multi-start single-flip local-search reference for $N\!\le\!16$ under order-2 modeling with $2^{5}{=}32$-phase dictionary while the order-4 model shows a performance ceiling below the classical reference. The approach suggests a route to near-optimal large-$N$ performance on future fault-tolerant (FTQ) quantum computers, which enable the higher-depth QAOA circuits.
summary: This work proposes an advanced method to solve the NP-hard phase optimization problem in RIS systems by designing QAOA angles offline using theoretical limits from spin-glass models. The approach successfully transfers these pre-calculated, channel-independent angles to simulate performance across various complex wireless fading environments. It suggests a viable path toward near-optimal power aggregation achievable only on future fault-tolerant quantum computers.
main_problem: The core problem is optimizing the aggregate received power for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) by setting discrete per-element phases, which is an NP-hard combinatorial optimization task.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that an offline, channel-independent angle dictionary derived from infinite-size spin-glass limits can achieve near-optimal performance across various realistic fading channels for small system sizes ($N \le 16$).
method: They formulate the problem as a QUBO/HUBO and employ QAOA with angles pre-optimized offline using techniques derived from Basso et al.'s infinite-size Gaussian ensemble benchmark.
model_or_system: The system is an RIS array whose phase optimization objective ($\max \|A e^{j	heta}\|^2$) is mapped onto a spin Hamiltonian. The theoretical framework relies on relating this to the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model and its infinite-size limits.
key_observables: Performance ratios ($r_b, r_m$), which compare achieved power to the classical optimum; single-shot success probability ($P_{0.9}$).
important_parameters: QAOA depth ($p$), number of elements ($N$), dictionary size ($L=2^M$), and channel type (Rayleigh, Rician/LOS, etc.).
main_assumptions: The method is designed for the Fault-Tolerant Quantum (FTQ) regime; it relies on reducing the high-order Hamiltonian to a manageable order-2 Ising surrogate.
figures_summary: Figures compare performance ratios ($r_b, r_m$) vs. QAOA depth ($p$) for both order-2 and order-4 models across different channel types (e.g., Fig. 7 compares $N=12$ transfer).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical problem, derives the necessary Hamiltonian formulation, details the offline angle dictionary construction using infinite-size limits ($V_p$), and validates this approach by testing its robustness across multiple complex channel models via numerical simulations.
why_interesting: It bridges quantum optimization theory (spin glasses, QAOA) with a highly relevant applied physics problem (wireless communications/RIS), providing concrete benchmarks for future fault-tolerant quantum hardware applications in electromagnetics.
